78.title: Three companions
78.hook: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala are killed in Delhi for refusing to give up their faith
78.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala among the martyrs recalled in the Ardas, and a museum and memorials near Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi honor them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pandits of Kashmir, led by Kirpa Ram, who traveled to Anandpur for help. Your line was they came to him. Did you stop and really listen to someone? Day seventy-eight.

This is a hard day in the story, and we'll walk through it gently. After listening to the pandits, Guru Tegh Bahadur decided to go to Delhi himself, to stand for them before the emperor. He did not go alone. A few close companions went with him, men who had served him for years. Tradition says they were arrested on the way and brought to Delhi in chains. The authorities wanted the Guru to give up his faith, and he would not. So, tradition says, they tried to break him by making him watch what happened to his friends. Today, three names Sikhs say with love.
screen: `A HARD DAY, WALKED GENTLY.` → `ARRESTED ON THE ROAD.` → `THREE FRIENDS OF THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Their names were Bhai Mati Das, his younger brother Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala. Bhai means brother, the title Sikhs give to respected members of the community. Mati Das and Sati Das were brothers from a Brahmin family who served as the Guru's close aides and scribes. Dayala was a devoted companion from the same circle. In Delhi, in November 1675, each of them was offered the same bargain: give up your faith and live. Each refused. And each was put to death, tradition says in front of the Guru, in the old city, near where Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands today. Tradition remembers the manner of each death in painful detail, and Sikhs recall it every year. We'll only say this much: they were killed with great cruelty, and they did not bend. What Sikhs hold onto is how they faced it. Tradition says Bhai Mati Das was reciting the Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, which you met near the start of this path, and kept reciting to the end. Tradition says each of the three stayed calm, and kept the Name. Notice something else: none of them was a Guru. They were ordinary members of the community, a scribe, his brother, a friend, and they are remembered today in the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say together, among those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. The Sikh story honors not only its Gurus, but the companions who stood beside them.

Let the three names move slowly through your mind: Mati Das. Sati Das. Dayala. Then let your thoughts widen to anyone, anywhere, who has suffered for holding to what they believe. You don't need words. Just keep the flame company, and breathe. The bell holds the time.

79.title: Chandni Chowk, 1675
79.hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur is beheaded in Delhi for defending others' freedom to practice their faith
79.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year with prayers, processions and recitation, and many visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, where he was beheaded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three companions: Mati Das, Sati Das and Dayala. Your line was they did not bend. Did you stand by a friend when stepping back was easier? Day seventy-nine.

Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi, on an ordinary afternoon. The street is packed: rickshaws, spice sellers, wedding shops, sweet shops, horns, a river of people. In the middle of it all stands a gurdwara with a gold dome, Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib. Sis means head. People step in off the noise, cover their heads, and go quiet. They are standing on the spot where, in November 1675, a Guru was put to death, not for his own community, but for someone else's. Today, what happened in the square.
screen: `A PACKED STREET IN OLD DELHI.` → `A GOLD DOME: SIS GANJ.` → `NOVEMBER 1675.`

segments.voice: The name Chandni Chowk is usually explained as the moonlit square. In 1675 it was the grand market street of the Mughal capital. Tradition says that Guru Tegh Bahadur, held in Delhi, was given the same choice as his companions: accept Islam, or show a miracle to prove his standing, or die. He refused all three. He would not give up his faith, and he would not perform wonders on demand. And so, in the open square, in November 1675, the ninth Guru was beheaded. Now remember why he had come. The pandits of Kashmir were Hindus. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, which the Gurus had not taken up. The Guru did not share their practices. He gave his life for their right to keep them. His son, who became the tenth Guru, later wrote about his father's death in a poem called Bachitar Natak. He says, in plain words, that his father protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread, and did a great deed in this dark age. That he gave his head, but not his faith. Sikhs gave Guru Tegh Bahadur a title because of this: Hind di chadar, the shield of India, the sheet that covered and protected people. Here's what's worth carrying tonight. It is one thing to die for your own faith. It is something else to die so that people who believe differently from you may believe freely. That is what Sikhs remember in the square every year.
screen: `CHANDNI CHOWK — THE MOONLIT SQUARE.` · `NO CONVERSION, NO MIRACLES.` · `HE GAVE HIS HEAD, NOT HIS FAITH.` · `HIND DI CHADAR, THE SHIELD.` · then, large: `FOR ANOTHER'S FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone else's freedom in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of people, somewhere in the world, who aren't free to practice their faith, or to live by their conscience. They may believe very differently from you. Hold them in mind without needing to agree with them. If you pray, you can pray for their freedom in whatever words are yours. If you don't, just wish it for them, sincerely, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
Chandni Chowk. The moonlit square in Old Delhi where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded in 1675, defending others' freedom to practice their faith.
Your line: for another's faith. Today, speak up once, kindly, for someone whose beliefs differ from yours. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: Carrying the head home
80.hook: Bhai Jaita carries the Guru's head to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah burns his own house to cremate the body
80.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Jaita and Lakhi Shah Vanjara at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Anandpur Sahib, where the head was cremated, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj in Delhi, where the body was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chandni Chowk, where the ninth Guru gave his head but not his faith. Your line was for another's faith. Did you speak up for someone who believes differently? Day eighty.

When someone dies far from home, someone has to bring them back. Anyone who has done it knows: the paperwork, the long drive, the phone calls, the sitting with the body. It's one of the most loving and least noticed jobs there is. After the Guru was killed in Chandni Chowk, his body lay in the square under guard. Tradition says the authorities meant it as a warning, and that nobody dared go near it. The Sikhs in Delhi were watched and afraid. And yet two men, on the same night, decided the Guru would not be left there. Today, the brave, quiet work of bringing him home.
screen: `SOMEONE HAS TO BRING THEM BACK.` → `THE BODY IN THE SQUARE.` → `TWO MEN, ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The first was Bhai Jaita, a Sikh from a community that society treated as low caste. Tradition says that in the confusion of a dust storm that night, he slipped through, took up the Guru's head, wrapped it, and set off for Anandpur, hundreds of miles away, traveling in secret, mostly at night. When he arrived, the young Gobind Rai, now the tenth Guru at nine years old, received his father's head. Tradition says he embraced Jaita and spoke a line Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas, Jaita's own community, are the Guru's own sons. A boy honoring a man the world looked down on, calling him family. Jaita later took initiation and became Bhai Jiwan Singh. The second man was Lakhi Shah, a wealthy trader who carried goods by bullock cart. In the same storm, tradition says, he and his sons hid the Guru's body in a cart under a load of cotton, and drove it to their house outside the city. They couldn't hold a public cremation; soldiers would have come. So Lakhi Shah built a pyre inside his own home, laid the Guru's body in it, and set his house on fire. To the neighbors, it looked like an accident. It was his home, given as a funeral. Today Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands there, near the Parliament of India. Two men. One carried the head to a nine-year-old son. One burned down everything he had. Neither was a Guru, and both brought him home. With them, the story of the ninth Guru ends.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a brave, quiet kindness, starting with choosing one. Settle and breathe. Think of a loving task that nobody wants to do and nobody will thank you for. Visiting someone difficult. Sorting a relative's things. Sitting with someone in a hospital. Calling the family nobody calls. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without being seen, like a man walking through a dust storm. Let it feel possible. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Jaita. The Sikh who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head from Delhi to Anandpur, whom the young Guru called a son of the Guru.
Your line: bring him home. Today, do the loving task you thought of, or one step of it, and tell no one. Day eighty.

81.title: A child at Patna
81.hook: Gobind Rai is born in Patna in 1666 and grows up playing at archery by the Ganges
81.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's birth each year with prayers and processions, and many visit Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the birthplace, and the gurdwara of Rani Maini, where boiled chickpeas are given as prasad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, carrying the head home: Bhai Jaita, Lakhi Shah, and the end of the ninth Guru's story. Your line was bring him home. Did you do a quiet kindness no one saw? Day eighty-one.

Somewhere in your family there may be a story about you at three that comes out at every gathering. The time you tried to feed the dog your broccoli. The summer you only answered to the name of a superhero. Those stories are small, but they're how a family says: we knew you before you were anyone. Today begins the story of the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. Warrior, poet, founder of the Khalsa. But before any of that, there was a little boy in a city on the Ganges, far from Punjab, who had never met his father. Today, the child at Patna.
screen: `THE STORIES FAMILIES TELL.` → `THE TENTH GURU BEGINS.` → `A BOY ON THE GANGES.`

segments.voice: Remember day seventy-six: Guru Tegh Bahadur traveling east, leaving his wife, Mata Gujri, in Patna while he went on toward Assam. There, in Patna, in December 1666, their son was born. They named him Gobind Rai. His father was far away and would not see him for years. So the boy grew up with his mother, his grandmother Mata Nanaki and his uncle Kirpal Chand, among the Sikh families of a big city on a great river. Sikhs tell a handful of stories about those years, and they are full of play. The boy loved to lead the other children in mock battles, dividing them into two armies. He practiced archery by the river. Tradition says he would shoot small arrows, or toss things, at the women carrying water pots, cracking the pots, and his mother had to replace them. One story is especially tender. A local raja's wife, Rani Maini, had no children, and longed for a son. Tradition says the little boy came into her house and climbed into her lap, calling her mother, and she fed him boiled and salted chickpeas. At the gurdwara that stands there today, visitors are still given those chickpeas. In Patna the Sikh community remembers his birthplace with Takht Sri Patna Sahib, one of the five takhts. Hold onto this picture: a mischievous, warm, sporty boy, loved by a whole neighborhood. Around 1672 he was brought to Punjab, to his father at Anandpur. Everything else comes later.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a game you loved. Settle and breathe. Go back to being small. What did you play? Tag in the street. Pretend kitchens. A ball against a wall. Building forts out of couch cushions. Let one game come back in detail: the place, the other kids, the rules you made up, how it felt to be completely absorbed. Let yourself smile if you want to. Stay there a moment. The bell holds the time.

82.title: Who is worthier than you
82.hook: tradition says the nine-year-old told his father no one was worthier to answer the Kashmiris' plea
82.tomorrow: a court of poets at Anandpur
82.howItsDone: Sikhs often tell this story to children, and honor Guru Gobind Singh as the one who, at nine, encouraged his father to stand for the Kashmiri pandits.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child at Patna Sahib: armies of children, archery by the Ganges, chickpeas in Rani Maini's lap. Your line was the boy by the river. Did you do one thing just for fun? Day eighty-two.

Sometimes a child says the thing the adults have been circling for hours. The family is arguing about whether to move grandma in, and a seven-year-old says, well, she's lonely, isn't she? The room goes quiet. Everyone knew. Nobody had said it. Go back to day seventy-seven: Anandpur, 1675. The pandits of Kashmir have told their story. The Guru is sitting in silence, heavy with it. The boy from Patna is about nine now, living with his father at last. He walks in, sees his father's face, and asks what's wrong. Today, what the nine-year-old said.
screen: `A CHILD SAYS WHAT EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `BACK TO ANANDPUR, 1675.` → `WHAT'S WRONG, FATHER?`

segments.voice: Here is the exchange as Sikh tradition tells it. The boy asks his father why he is so quiet. Guru Tegh Bahadur explains, simply, what the pandits have come for: they're being forced to give up their faith, and nobody can protect them. And then he says the hard part out loud. It would take the sacrifice of a great and holy person to stop this. The boy thinks about it, the way children do, completely seriously. And he answers: who could be worthier than you, father? That's the whole story. A handful of words from a nine-year-old. Tradition is clear that the boy understood what he was saying. He was offering his father. And his father heard it not as a child's mistake, but as an answer. Tradition says the Guru was glad, because he saw that his son was ready to lead. He told the pandits to go to the authorities and say: if Guru Tegh Bahadur accepts conversion, we all will. Then he named Gobind Rai as the next Guru, and set out for Delhi, knowing where the road went. You already know the rest. What Sikhs take from this moment is the courage of the boy. A child of nine gave up his father for people who weren't even his community, because it was right. That boy became the tenth Guru. The line people carry from it is simpler: when something needs doing, and you're wondering who should do it, sometimes the honest answer is: who better than you?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone who faces something hard. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone standing at the edge of something difficult: a surgery, a hard conversation, a new job, a decision they're afraid of. Picture their face. Then picture yourself saying to them, simply and warmly: you can do this. Who better than you? Notice how it feels to believe in someone out loud. Let that settle in. The bell holds the time.
Gobind Rai. The tenth Guru's name as a boy, who at nine years old told his father there is no one worthier than you.
Your line: who better than you. Today, send the person you thought of a message of real encouragement. Day eighty-two.

83.title: A court of poets at Anandpur
83.hook: the young Guru gathers poets and scholars, writes himself, and fights at Bhangani in 1688
83.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the Jaap Sahib, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, in their daily morning prayers, and Paonta Sahib on the Yamuna is visited as the place where he wrote much of his poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is worthier than you: Gobind Rai's answer to his father. Your line was who better than you. Did you encourage someone facing something hard? Day eighty-three.

Nine years old, a father executed in Delhi, and a whole community now looking to you. A child like that could grow up hard, angry, all armor. The young Guru Gobind Rai did grow up strong. He trained in riding, archery and the sword, and the hill rajas around Anandpur watched him with suspicion. But he also did something unexpected. He filled his court with poets. Musicians, scholars, translators, writers of every background came to Anandpur, and the Guru wrote alongside them. Today, the young Guru with a pen in one hand and a sword in the other.
screen: `NINE, AND FATHERLESS.` → `TRAINING IN ARMS.` → `AND A COURT FULL OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the Guru kept fifty-two poets at his court. They translated old stories and epics into the language people spoke, wrote verse about heroes and about God, and made Anandpur, a small hill town, into a center of learning. The Guru himself wrote, in several languages: in Braj, a literary Hindi of the time, in Persian, and in Punjabi. For some years he lived at Paonta, a quiet spot on the Yamuna river, where tradition says much of his early poetry was written. Many of his writings were later gathered into a book called the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth. Many Sikhs recite some of its hymns daily, like the Jaap Sahib. Scholars and Sikhs discuss how much of the whole collection comes from the Guru's own pen, and that conversation continues. Then, in 1688, the sword. A hill raja, Fateh Shah, with allied rajas, marched against the Guru, and they met at Bhangani, near Paonta. The Guru's force was small, and here Sikhs tell a detail worth keeping. A Muslim Sufi saint, Pir Budhu Shah, came to fight on the Guru's side, with his sons and hundreds of his followers. Tradition says two of his sons were killed in the battle. The Guru won, and tradition says he gave the Pir a gift in thanks: his own comb, with strands of his hair still in it, and a turban. The young Guru held both, the pen and the sword, and neither canceled the other. The poet fought. The fighter wrote about God.
screen: `FIFTY-TWO POETS AT ANANDPUR.` · `THE GURU WRITES IN THREE LANGUAGES.` · `BHANGANI, 1688.` · `PIR BUDHU SHAH FIGHTS BESIDE HIM.` · then, large: `PEN AND SWORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of poetry. Find any poem: a book on your shelf, a hymn, a song lyric you love, even a line you half remember. Read or say one line slowly. Then again, slower. Let each word land. Then close your eyes and sit with it. Notice how a single line can hold more than a whole paragraph. Let it echo while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Dasam Granth. The book of the tenth, gathering much of Guru Gobind Singh's own writing, from the years his court at Anandpur was full of poets.
Your line: pen and sword. Today, balance a hard task with something beautiful: read a poem, sing, write a line of your own. Day eighty-three.

84.title: Vaisakhi, 1699: the call
84.hook: before a great crowd the Guru draws his sword and asks who will give their head
84.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi each April as the birth of the Khalsa, with gurdwara services, processions called nagar kirtan, and, for many, taking amrit on or near the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a court of poets at Anandpur, the Dasam Granth, and a Sufi saint at Bhangani. Your line was pen and sword. Did you balance something hard with something beautiful? Day eighty-four.

Seven days, in one breath. Three companions who did not bend. A Guru who gave his head in Chandni Chowk for another's faith. Two men who carried him home. A boy by the river in Patna. His answer to his father. The court of poets. Everything in the story so far has been building to one morning. It's spring, 1699, at Anandpur. The harvest festival of Vaisakhi. The Guru has sent word across Punjab and beyond: come. And they come, in huge numbers, tens of thousands, tradition says, filling the hillside. They expect hymns, a festival, a blessing. The Guru steps out before them with a drawn sword. Today, the call.
screen: `A WEEK THAT BUILDS TO ONE MORNING.` → `ANANDPUR, SPRING 1699.` → `A DRAWN SWORD.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival of Punjab, when the wheat is cut, held in the month of Vaisakh, usually around the middle of April. Long before 1699 it was a time of fairs and gatherings. After 1699 it became something more for Sikhs: the birthday of the Khalsa. Here's what happened, as Sikh tradition tells it. The Guru stood before the crowd, sword raised, and asked a question no one there expected. Is there anyone here who will give me their head? Silence. Nobody moved. He asked again. Then a third time. Finally one man stood up: Daya Ram, a shopkeeper from Lahore. The Guru took him into a tent. There was a sound. The Guru came out alone, with blood on his sword, and asked again: who else will give their head? People began to slip away, frightened. Some went to the Guru's mother to complain he'd lost his mind. And still, a second man stood. Then a third. A fourth. A fifth. Each went into the tent. Each time the Guru came out alone. What happened inside the tent? The sources don't say clearly, and Sikhs tell it in more than one way. Some tellings say the Guru truly took their lives and restored them. Others say the five were never harmed and the blood was from goats, a test of faith all along. Some Sikhs simply leave the tent closed. What matters is the question, and the five who answered it. Tomorrow, the tent opens.
screen: `VAISAKHI — THE HARVEST FESTIVAL.` · `WHO WILL GIVE ME THEIR HEAD?` · `DAYA RAM STANDS FIRST.` · `FIVE GO INTO THE TENT.` · then, large: `WHO WILL GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with what you'd give everything for. Settle and breathe. Let the Guru's question come to you gently, not as a demand, just as a question. What in your life matters so much you'd give everything for it? A person. A value. A faith. A child. You don't need to answer quickly. Let the answer rise, or not. Just sit on the hillside with the question, the way the crowd did, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Vaisakhi. The spring harvest festival of Punjab, and for Sikhs, the day in 1699 when the Guru asked who would give their head.
Your line: who will give. Today, when something needs a volunteer, a task, a hand, a first step, be the one who stands up. Day eighty-four, the end of another week.
